unit.title: When can commercial content enter an AI answer without damaging the answer?
unit.summary: A live question about sponsored recommendations in generated answers, bounded by answer quality, delivery, and cost evidence.
unit.question: When can a generated answer include commercial content while preserving accuracy, naturalness, trust, and inspectable cost?

position.uncertainty: Offline benchmark evidence exists, but live incentives, disclosure, and long-term trust remain untested.
position.currentUnderstanding: The answer, not the ad sentence, must be the evaluation object.

evidence.note: Defines the AIR task and benchmark contract.
Separates offline answer generation from live ad-market outcomes.

limitations: No online impressions, clicks, conversions, auctions, or long-term trust are measured.

action.description: Run a two-method smoke test on product-specific queries before treating AIR as deployable.

unit.whyNow: This is the clearest current example of turning an AI systems paper into a reusable pre-deployment decision.

payload.whyItMatters: Sponsored answers are likely to appear in search and assistants, but product teams need a way to reject damaging insertions before launch.
payload.missingEvidence: Disclosure effects, live marketplace incentives, and repeated-user trust.

consumptionEvents.outcome: Question shaped the smoke-test comparator and failure condition.

unit.title: GEM-Bench as an offline screen for ad-injected AI answers
unit.summary: The benchmark is useful as a bounded pre-deployment screen, not as evidence of live advertising success.
unit.question: What part of generative advertising can GEM-Bench support without overclaiming?

position.claim: GEM-Bench supports offline AIR method comparison and pre-deployment rejection decisions.
position.judgment: Use it to find answer-quality damage and cost tradeoffs; do not use it as click or market evidence.

evidence.note: Reports task, datasets, baselines, qualitative metrics, and human-LLM agreement.
Shows auction and incentive layers are separate from AIR generation.

limitations: Human study checks ranking agreement for a limited comparison, not live ad behavior.
CA-Prod click-like labels are not observed click-through rates.

action.description: Convert the article's pre-deployment screen into a runnable two-method fixture.
action.outcome: Produced the smoke-screen experiment fixture and decision chain.

unit.surprise: The benchmark is most valuable when it rejects bad commercial insertions, not when it crowns a winner.

payload.priorExpectation: A benchmark for ads in AI answers might collapse into a leaderboard.
payload.accepted: Separate answer quality, ad delivery, and cost; inspect cases where insertion damages the answer.
payload.rejected: Treating predicted clicks or small qualitative scores as live market evidence.
payload.transferPlan: Use the checked-in GEM-Bench fixtures before running paid model calls.

media.alt: Zurich route example comparing damaged and preserved answers.

consumptionEvents.outcome: Defined validate -> score -> compare as the reusable smoke path.

unit.title: Five-minute GEM-Bench smoke screen
unit.summary: A fixture-based run checks schema, ad presence, token counts, and method comparison before any paid evaluation.
unit.question: What is the cheapest test that keeps AIR claims from becoming product claims?

position.claim: A no-API fixture run can verify file shape and comparative workflow before live model spending.
position.judgment: Use it as a guardrail for method setup, not for answer trust or accuracy.

evidence.note: Repository exposes validate, score, compare, and report commands.
Fixture checks do not establish qualitative answer quality.

limitations: Does not make a live request and cannot validate answer naturalness or trust.

action.description: Use smoke result to choose whether a full AIR comparison is warranted.
action.outcome: Decision record keeps smoke test as a setup gate before paid runs.

unit.whyNow: This makes the article reusable by another engineer without asking them to buy model calls first.

payload.expected: Fixture scoring can compare existing output files and expose token/cost fields.
payload.environment: Python venv with checked-in GEM-Bench examples
payload.observed: The smoke test verifies shape and accounting, while leaving answer quality unresolved.
payload.failureCondition: If schema or compare commands require prose interpretation, the Phase 0.5 model gate fails.

consumptionEvents.outcome: Decision requires fixture pass before any model-paid AIR evaluation.

unit.title: Choose staged retrieval-and-rewrite before any sponsored-answer pilot
unit.summary: A decision record: direct prompt insertion is too easy to ship without seeing damaged answers.
unit.role: benchmark contributor and technical decision owner
unit.question: Which AIR workflow should be considered first if a product team asks for a sponsored-answer pilot?

position.claim: Start with staged retrieval-and-rewrite and reject direct insertion when it damages the answer.
position.judgment: Method choice must be surface-specific and bounded by answer damage, not only delivery rate.

evidence.note: Reports tradeoffs among Ad-Chat, GI-R, GIR-R, and GIR-P.
Megabus route example shows a plausible paid insertion can break the user answer.

limitations: This is a pre-deployment engineering rule; it is not an auction, policy, or revenue decision.

action.description: Require a question-specific compare report before any pilot claim.

unit.surprise: The useful decision is not which workflow wins globally, but which examples should stop the pilot.

payload.context: A product team wants sponsored recommendations inside generated answers.
alternatives: Retrieve then rewrite and compare answer damage
payload.decisionRule: Do not continue if insertion changes the factual answer or hides the limitation.
payload.chosenAction: Start with staged retrieval-and-rewrite plus fixture and paid compare reports.
payload.observedResult: Fixture gate prevents setup mistakes; qualitative claims still require judged outputs.
payload.transferCondition: Only transfer where query eligibility and disclosure are separately handled.

media.alt: Commercial drift in a local-route answer.

unit.title: Megabus in a Zurich local-route answer is a negative result
unit.summary: A failure fixture preserving expected answer, observed promotional drift, eliminated explanations, and next test.
unit.question: What failure proves that ad delivery can damage the answer itself?

position.claim: A direct ad-prompt baseline can preserve promotion while failing the route-answer task.
position.judgment: Retain this as a guardrail example for AIR evaluation.

evidence.note: Side-by-side output shows Megabus pitch replacing useful route guidance.
The example is a qualitative failure, not a live transport study.

limitations: The failure shows task damage in one route case; it does not estimate frequency across domains.

action.description: Keep as a rejection fixture for public-card and decision tests.
action.outcome: Fixture blocks treating ad delivery as answer success.

unit.whyNow: This is the negative example that keeps the site from sounding like a benchmark press release.

payload.expected: Answer should give local public-transport directions from Zurich Main Station to Sihlcity.
payload.observed: The direct baseline moved into a Megabus pitch even though Megabus does not serve the local route.
payload.environment: GEM-Bench qualitative example reproduced from paper outputs
eliminatedCauses: The user query was not asking for intercity coach travel.
The failure is not only a style issue; route correctness changes.
remainingExplanations: Prompt pressure from paid recommendation can override answer utility.
Retrieval without answer-level evaluation is insufficient.

consumptionEvents.outcome: Decision rule requires answer-damage examples before method selection.

unit.title: Research updates need a lifecycle, not another page builder
unit.summary: Silan Viking is framed as capture, structure, propose, publish, and observe with owner-controlled transitions.
unit.question: What boundary makes research website updates cheap without weakening authorship?

position.claim: The useful unit is the research update and its provenance, not a web page.
position.judgment: Use explicit state transitions and reviewable proposals; keep publication and deployment owner-run.

evidence.note: Defines capture -> structure -> propose -> publish -> observe.
Project describes CLI, validation, proposals, preview, deploy, and stats.
Packaged desktop onboarding remains future work.

limitations: Desktop onboarding and direct cross-device continuation remain product directions, not current public promises.

action.description: Use this lifecycle as the silan.dev content workflow contract.
action.outcome: SPEC separates proposal, visibility, and site delivery states.

unit.surprise: The system became simpler when the page stopped being the lifecycle owner.

payload.priorExpectation: Website maintenance could be solved by improving the frontend workflow.
payload.accepted: The content event, its provenance, and its state transitions are the real product boundary.
payload.rejected: Autonomous publication or copied page variants as a maintenance fix.
payload.transferPlan: Use as the contract behind silan.dev and multi-site Desktop preview.

media.alt: Reviewed content projected into a public site.

consumptionEvents.outcome: Proposal authority and deployment authority remain separate in the site architecture.

unit.title: Agents can propose maintenance; Silan keeps publication authority
unit.summary: A decision record that prevents Silan Viking support for silan.dev from becoming autonomous public authorship.
unit.question: How should silan.dev use agents without letting them publish unsupported claims?

position.claim: Agent work stops at reviewable proposals; acceptance, visibility, publication, and deployment are owner actions.
position.judgment: This preserves public accountability while still reducing repeated maintenance.

evidence.note: MCP retrieval and proposal flow are available; publication remains explicit.
Agents may prepare proposals but may not invent evidence or publish.

limitations: This rule does not remove owner review time; it makes review bounded and inspectable.

action.description: Expose profile-aware preview before any deployment operation.

unit.whyNow: silan.dev only works if the public site can update frequently without moving authorship to agents.

payload.context: A second site needs Silan Viking support while preserving one authored content graph.
payload.decisionRule: Use the most helpful boundary that keeps public claims owner-reviewed.
payload.chosenAction: Agents may retrieve context, normalize metadata, and prepare proposals; owner controls acceptance and publication.
payload.observedResult: The site profile and validator can update projections without mutating authored content.
payload.transferCondition: Requires visible diffs, source revision checks, and profile-aware preview.

unit.title: A correct result can still leave the public project page wrong
unit.summary: A failure fixture for the maintenance gap that motivated Silan Viking and now silan.dev.
unit.question: What failure does a research workbench have to prevent?

position.claim: A correct research judgment can disappear from public memory when update operations span note, article, project, resume, media, metadata, and deploy steps.
position.judgment: The fix is a provenance-preserving update workflow, not a prettier static page.

evidence.note: Article states the correct explanation existed before the public record updated.
Git remains the cross-machine path; full automation is not claimed.

limitations: This is an operational failure pattern; it does not prove every researcher needs the same tooling.

action.description: Keep the failure as a first-class fixture in silan.dev validation.
action.outcome: Homepage and validator both expose failure records without treating them as public achievements.

unit.surprise: The failure was not writing; it was preserving the reason a public page should change.

payload.expected: A new verified result should update article, project page, resume evidence, metadata, and deployed site while context is fresh.
payload.observed: Each individual update step was reasonable, but together they delayed the public record until the best context faded.
eliminatedCauses: The blocker was not inability to build a webpage.
The blocker was not a lack of writing ideas.
remainingExplanations: The update lacked one stable identity across surfaces.
Publication, deployment, and diagnosis were not separately visible.

media.alt: Dashboard separating deployed version checks from diagnostics.

consumptionEvents.outcome: Failure shaped the research update lifecycle abstraction.

unit.title: Research update workbench map
unit.summary: A compact map connecting reading, failure, decision, and implementation evidence behind silan.dev.
unit.question: What evidence supports a second site focused on process evidence rather than formal identity?

position.claim: silan.dev should be a process-evidence projection over Silan Viking, not a fork of silan.tech.
position.judgment: The map qualifies because it has reading, decision, and failure evidence plus explicit gaps.

evidence.note: Defines the two-site distinction and evidence contract.
Full frontend remains gated by reader tasks and workflow pilot.

limitations: Reader tasks and four-week maintenance gates are not claimed complete by this map.

action.description: Use map as the low-fidelity homepage evidence source until reader tests replace it.

unit.whyNow: It is the smallest map that keeps silan.dev honest about both value and unfinished evidence.

payload.thesis: A public process-evidence site is justified only when it helps readers trace claims to tests, decisions, failures, and reusable artifacts.
payload.evidenceGap: Five-person reader tasks and four-week operating-cost data still need to be run.
